He cooked them. Burn them all. Yeah, yeah. But they were good. And I can remember ... we had peaches for years and years and years. Well, we didn't have money in that first place to buy peaches, you know. And I don't want to have any peaches to get either as far as I told you. I don't know about that. But I remember when the mother got the first peaches, she made some peach jam. Oh, I thought that was wonderful. We sat down on the water and warmed, and mother had made some fresh bread, put some butter on it and this peach jam on it. And she made her homemade cheese, you know. And that was good. Oh, she made a lot of homemade cheese out of the milk. And had that sitting out of the morning. And I still can remember that short plate. Sounds good. Yeah, it was good. It was really good.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did your father have fruit trees? Did your father have fruit trees? Orchard or anything? Did he have an orchard?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah, he had an orchard. He had all kinds of apples, prunes, cherries, and some pear trees. The no peach trees. No, no, no, peaches. Oh, no, they were used over here. It was too cold to freeze up. In the wintertime. pear tree do very good eating. We had a plan of the pear tree up in the house, and we got one year, one box of pear tree that they died at, and it was just too cold weather. Two years. And there was two rows for it. They should have been up higher. And ours in the backyard is low. So we don't have anything to do.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: What did you do about vegetables when you were young?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: We always raised carrots. We had carrots, and we had cabbage, as long as it lasted. And of course, we had always ramen in the fall. And it lasted quite a while. Carrots, we had mayo, bib, and I don't know how big. About from here over there, we were up as high as the refrigerator for a carrot. That's right. Oh, yeah, there was a big sale out of carrots. Wow, they had carrots.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: And they just stayed, you left them outside?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah, that was in the big summer, and they didn't freeze there. Oh. Yeah. We had plenty of carrots and cabbage. Yeah. And there was potatoes. Potatoes, you know, the main thing. And then we had, of course, our milk in there. And I remember, they had screen doors in front of the milk for a flight to get in. And the milk had to be raised, you know, and that mother had skimmed the cream off. You had no separator or anything like that at that time. So it just skimmed off, and she'd make butter. And she'd make butter to sell, too. Oh, she made about 16, 16 pounds a week. Returned and made butter. It was good butter. She was a good butter maker.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: How many cows did you have? ... How many cows?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, we had eight cows. I milked two in the morning, my sister, two, and my brother. I didn't make six. And we'd give up early and milked two cows and come up and that's when we had to begin to get our separator. So then we'd separate and bring the milk and feed the calves, come back in and get ready, hang over the school, and walk a mile and a quarter over the dirt.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Those were your chores then?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Those are chores.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you have inside chores, too? Did you have to make your bed before you went and stuff like that? Bed for the cows?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: No, no. Your bed in the house. Oh, we didn't have time for that.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: So mother did that?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: No. Well, we didn't sometimes ever do it because it wasn't time. Mother had to do with the dishes, she had to get the food ready, eat when we got home. So we'd just crawl back in bed the way it was. Oh, okay. I see. Oh, it wasn't too bad. Once a week we'd change it and make it on Saturday. And sometimes you'd make it in between, but that was very often. A lot of time for it. The time you milk two cows and feed them separate and you go feed the cows, and come in and get ready for school, and you had to be ready to go to school at eight o 'clock. Uh-huh. That was one of many times.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: And then you had that long walk, too.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Remember, we used to get on top of the hill and we'd hear the bell ring, and we'd run down. And of course there's Bob Barr fans as we'd put sacks on the Bob Barr so we could go through without jarring our tolls. But, uh, yeah, I got in, and I don't know who made the fire for the teacher. Maybe one of the people that lived closer, or she did maybe, I don't know. But it was a warm hot fire I could get inside.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: You looked forward to getting to the choir?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: And I see Sir Ol Carter. I read him a article. The other day I thought there was real interesting. Benjamin Franklin. Uh-huh. He was only three years old. He was in the third grade, and he had to quit school. Third grade. And I think I have it here. And he worked around, and he didn't like it there. So he left, I think he was born in Boston or went to Boston, to Philadelphia, or vice versa. I don't remember enough. But anyway, he got books and studied himself. Uh-huh. And, uh... ... so I could read it better. Oh! Church Hill. This is Church Hill. I thought I'd be there in Franklin. I guess I have nothing. I should have it somewhere. But this is interesting, too, Church Hill. You remember Church Hill, I imagine.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: You remember Church Hill?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah… oh, yeah, I remember him in the war. He was a good... I'll just read what he said. Church Hill was invited to speak at his old school at Harrell. The headmaster told the boys that a great statesman was coming, and that was a great event that would give them a marvelous message that they would never forget, that this would take them through life successfully while the old man came. He was 89 years old at the time. As he stood before the boys, he ... down on the end of his nose. He looked over the audience. The boys were sitting on the same bench as he himself had carved his initials long ago. He was silent for a moment and began his marvelous message, one that ought to be given to boys today. It was never then a silence. Never. He boomed again. Never, never give in. Then he sat down. That was an entire speech. Hmm.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: But they remembered that. He didn't say much, but it didn't take much to say much. It didn't take much.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: It carved in the benches his initials, huh?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you put your initials in the school desk?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah, I did. I don't know if I did or not. Oh, I wasn't so good either, but... Yeah. That is something. That's right. I marched it there. Hmm. But Benjamin Franklin, on his message, he was three years old. No, that isn't the way it was. He was in the third grade, and he quit school. But I guess he didn't get along as well at home or something. I don't know. Anyway, he was born in Philadelphia or Boston or vice versa. And then he went there, and we got there where he was. He got in with a family, an English family, and they helped him, and he studied. And I think he did... He invented life-focused classes. I don't know. Everything at the time, he invented. Yeah. I suppose he was right there. He discovered electricity. Yeah. He interested in life-focused classes. And then he had to give a name for everything. Even in the motor of the car and everything, he had to give names to it. Find names to give to everything he made. There was no such thing before, so he had to. Right.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: ... Yeah, he was a wonderful man.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Do you remember when electricity came to this area?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: I can't remember when electricity was back. I remember when the telephone come in lately. Uh-huh. We had laps. I don't remember exactly when electricity came in, but I remember having laps. Then we got gasoline laps, the old-fashioned one, which gives them more light. And we had those a long time. I can't remember exactly when they got electricity, but it was quite a while.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did they have electricity in the city of Moscow before the farms?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Well, I think they ... I don't know. They must have though, I guess. I don't know. David had laps to run off or a crate. I can't remember. I was in the store sometimes, but not very much. They must have had some light, some way. They probably had laps. I suppose that's what it was.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: I wanted to go back and see if you could remember some of the things about how your mother made cheese. By what? You said your mother made cheese?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah… oh, yeah, you had to have milk. You had to have probably a bit of milk, at least three, four gallons anyway at the time, or probably more if you had. And that had to be lukewarm, and then you put the rennet in it. And then that would separate the milk. The cheesy stuff would go at the bottom of my nut and the other ... what do you call it? Water, right? It isn't that. But it would go at the top, and you skim that off. You could boil that down and make what they call Bruno's stone sweet. I don't know what it was. But they didn't ... most of them threw it out, I think.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: ... Yeah. That's a Swedish word for whatever the stuff was after it was boiled out. Yeah, that's good.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: And then she had a pan and a cloth, and you'd pack that cheese in there, and every day she had to change that cloth and rinse it off and put cheese back again until it got hard enough so she could put it out if it wasn't dry. It got real hard.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Now what type of cheese would this be? Do you remember her calling it that?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, it was just lukewarm. When you start to put the rennet in, I don't know exactly what temperature it was. Yeah, it is. Yeah, just lukewarm.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you like the stuff that was boiled? The ...?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah, it was pretty good. Pretty good. I didn't catch so much for it, but some people liked it. And some of the old people thought it was wonderful, but I liked the other cheese better. But mother had made, oh, a 10, 15 cheese when they had a lot of milk. Had all summer long.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: So she'd make the cheese in the summer.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: And then you'd keep it all year. Oh, I would keep that because it was dry just like other cheese, you know. It was hard on the outside, and you'd put it into it or, you know, softer. You'd slice it nicely. So it wasn't ... and they'd do that with meat, too. They'd dry the meat. And then they could cut it, slice it, thin slice it. And that was good, too. Mm. That beef, you could do that with. I guess they could do it with other people. I really didn't beat. I guess they did some with –… i don't know. Not part, but some other meats sometimes. I think deer, I think, they did some.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you eat much deer? ... Did you eat much deer at the time?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: No. I don't know. We ever ate any deer. Because we had the other meat, and I don't think they ... Well, I don't know if they had guns not to shoot a deer, or not. At the time. Yeah. So, well, I guess they didn't have guns. So, I remember they tried to shoot the pig, and so it was going to kill it. Then they had to have hot water in order to run it up and down, and so they could get that shave afterwards, you see. Wow. They had a sort of a thing they put, a big, great, big barrel. And then they had it sliding up so they could pull it in and out, so then they could pull it off. They could pull the hair off, but then it was done enough. So then afterwards they could shave it with a knife.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: They were taking the skin off, or just the hair?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: No, just the hair. ... Uh-huh. Huh. Yeah, a lot of that. And the skin got real clean, you know, white. It really looked good, so. So, it just, uh... Oh, there's a lot of tricks in that that start in. I kind of like to start over again, see how it... Oh, you do now. Well, you don't do any of that. No, I don't want to do that. At all. I can't do anything now. I just don't hardly walk. My legs are so poor. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Sounds like your mother had an awful lot of work.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Huh?

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Sounds like your mother had an awful lot of work. Oh, it did.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: An awful lot of work. Get the meals and the... I picked the berries in the summertime and canned them. We had a lot of raspberries and black caps, and they had to be picked and canned. I picked a lot of raspberries. I liked to pick raspberries. And black caps, and some are between black caps and others that they had too. And, uh... Oh, they really made that nice sauce in the summertime. A lot of good fruit. We canned apples and we... Apples really tells them not to be cooked as you need them, but... She did make a lot of apple butter. And the raspberries. A lot of raspberries. Black caps. Yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Were these wild berries, or did your father plant them?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, we planted them. Oh, we don't have any wild berries. You could go out in the mountains and pick huckleberries and things. But that was later in years. We never did that. We were young. Had to be grown. I don't want to say it was an apple berry, but I guess it was, but nobody knew anything about it.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you ever have any Indians come through?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: We had... My uncle, Nils Pearson, got a gun from the government. So if any Indians come, he could shoot them. Oh. And my store, they're up on the west. It's up on Hay Street. There used to be a house there. On the top was built. A great big... tight-seating place on top. It was round and windows all around, and they could go up there to see the Indians come. They could shoot them.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, they were afraid of Indians.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, they were afraid of them. They had Indians now. I'm worried that they have that good eating place now. Between Moscow and Spokane. Oh, over towards Steptoe Butte. Right up there were a lot of Indians, and there was war up there. They had a rigor war up there. Yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But your uncle got a gun. He was afraid, huh?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah. The government gave them the guns. Oh. The government... The gun he had was given by the government. Hmm. And I think it's in the family, yeah. It was a while back, anyway. For keepsake. Hmm. Yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But your father didn't necessarily have a gun, except for...

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: So... I remember Dad... He had Dad to walk to town, and coming home when it was so dark that he couldn't see where he was going. So he slept in the haystack overnight. Or a straw stack or something. And the way it was more, he could see where he was. No. So he got up and finished the walk home. For once, it had to come hard to start with. And no horses to drive. They had the horses, but they couldn't drive too dirty or too much snow or something. And we had a lot of snow. And they had no graders at that time, you know. Yeah. And just weights that melted. So... And then our way home, we had to follow clear around a long way, so you wouldn't have to climb that hill, because you couldn't ever make a hill. Because it wasn't graded, and there was the snow and there was a lot of ice on them. But later on in the years, they fixed that. And now they have a big road up there.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, that would be nice... Did you use sled in the winter? Did you sled in the winter? Scared? No, sleigh?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, we had our sleighs, yeah. Dad made sleighs. So we had to go up a hill and slide down. But it's funny, we didn't get killed, because of the ball bar fences those days, you know, because the cattle had cattle. But the sleigh, the snow was so high, we could go over the fences. It was so high and frozen. But when it started to go down, Dad was afraid that the horses would step on them and go down and get stuck in the wire fences. And he was afraid of us. Of course, when I got just a little bit, we screwed under. Oh, I'll never forget, Dad caught us riding a horse. They'd never been trained, you know. He'd go close to the fence and we'd climb up and go on his back. And Dad didn't know that for a long time. We had a lot of fun doing it. And then, you've seen us do it, and he stopped that. He said, that's dangerous. But the horse was just so good, he just walked around and we were on the back. We had two of them that way. And we had a lot of fun before you found out. But he found out and he put a stop to it.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: You were saying the snow used to get deep.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, cover the fence posts.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: How did you keep warm then? Keep warm. Walking to school.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, we had coal or wood in the house. In the house, yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But you still had to walk to school?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah. But we had long leggings, over shoes. We were just warm. You couldn't go like they do now, without pants legs or anything. Oh, no. You had wool stockings on. And then you had leggings like a king flare up with your butt left on the side or pull them on some way. And on big over shoes. Oh, we were well dressed for the weather.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you wear a skirt on top of that?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah, I was dressed. ... Yeah, we all wore dresses. Oh, we didn't wear any pants at that time. Remember the first lady in Spokane to put on pants was arrested. No kidding.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: No, no kidding. I'll be doggone.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Can you beat that?

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: I'd have a lot of arresting to do now.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah, they would. Yeah. I kept records on my husband when he was sick and my mother too. Bigger nurses records. Oh. And this is my husband's. Everything I did just like at a hospital.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you take care of him at home?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah… he threw a waste of anything. He's going to go down here. I said, well, you better save him. And he, oh, no, he said, when we get sick now, we'll have to go to the home. But he didn't want to go to the home when he got sick too. Yeah. And he threw away, he fixed up a chair for mother that she could use a pants slip under with the toilets, you know. And that was fine. And he had a nice ironing board. Oh, we don't need that anymore. He threw that out. Well, he got so sick of moving that it was everything you had to move, you know. So much stuff. After you've been at a place for so many years, then, well, he and his mother, his mother lived there first. And then, then, then the cousin of him lived there for a while. And he had a woman come in. And after that, we were married. First thing we got, we moved in. Have some more. Okay.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: So.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Do you remember hearing stories around about when Marshall Hayes was killed in Troy?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah. I don't already know about it, but he was shot. Mm-hmm. But who shot him? I don't know. But it's across the track somewhere around in there. It happened.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Now, it was still a big story by the time you got here 20 years later, huh?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah. I never had one. Another fellow. His name was Baylock on the way. To Troy. After you made this south opening of your turn west. They used to have a farmer's union there, a building. And he lived right around there. I guess they didn't like him very well. They put a, he sat in a chair and they put a bomb under his chair. And they shot him through the roof… oh… he just got splinters. He didn't kill him, but he just got splinters full of the, well, the roof and everything, you know.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: That's right. I heard that before. That's down where Cornwall. Yeah, yeah, that's it. Oh, yeah. Yeah. I'll be doggone. I guess they didn't like him. I don't know.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: But it's funny, he didn't kill him. He just put him right through the ceiling full of splinters. He had an arse, I guess, cup full of first placeers afterwards in his body. Poor guy. Well, let's see. You were a nurse before you came to Troy. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you work as a nurse in Troy when you were first born?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Well, I helped Dr. Myers with operations when he did here.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, he had a little hospital here?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah… ... I have a corner down here. Her name is... B. Roush. Oh, B. Roush. Yeah. Down in her house. That house was a hospital. Oh. I didn't know that.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: And this was Dr.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Myers. He moved, he quit here and moved to Seattle. But his wife died soon after he got to Seattle. And he had, he was diabetic. He had had both days amputated. So he sat in a chair the last few years. But he was diabetic when he was down here, but he had got some medicine. He tested his own urine, but the testing wasn't any good. So he never found out. So he kind of provoked to this, at the medicine he got, because he wouldn't know him himself. Because they finally got some other medicine, and he showed that he was diabetic. He was, because he had amputated both legs.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: What kind of operations did they do? This is like in the 1920s, I guess, isn't it? ... You worked for him in the, about 1920s?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah. Down here at the hospital, as long as he'd be here. Yeah. Okay.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did they have anesthesia and all that stuff?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yeah… he had another nurse named Mrs. Miller. She was a good person. She wasn't a graduate nurse, but she was good. After he stopped the anesthetics, then he switched over to her, and I helped him with the operations. Oh. Like some more Senka?

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Yeah. Here, I'll help myself. That warmed me up pretty good. Did you help deliver babies and things like that?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, yes… at the hospital at the manual, I helped him. I delivered some of the babies. I remember Dr. Dunn. Go ahead and deliver. He came and called him this time. I said, well, the baby's about here. Well, go ahead and deliver. So I did.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: That was the first time, huh?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: No, I remember it was the first time. There were several I did.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you ever do for people around here in their homes, or did they go to the hospital by then?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: No, not in my homes. I never did in my home. I helped with Mrs. Trier and watched her. I took care of her in the school on a program. He had tick cocks in her program. He ran over and his wife wasn't running back. Oh! I was with her, but there was a hard delivery. He had to use horses.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: I remember Trier said, well, can you do that?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Well, there's nothing else to do. Not only that, he just can't deliver. So years before, everything came out all right.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did your mother have doctors when she had her babies?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah, I had one. She had one named Delphine when I was born. Afterwards, it was Dr. Gritman. Oh, Asprey did too some. Dr. Asprey later came. He didn't, no, he's dead too. His son has got tick x-rays and spoke in at the medical building. So that's Melvin Asprey. He had two children, Dr. Asprey did. That was Melvin and Ruth. The girl's name was ... when she was married. But, oh, I don't know. I know I came into the hospital and a woman told me, she said, do you know that you was with my mother when I was born? That made me feel kind of old. Oh, I think there's so many I couldn't remember, you know, everybody I was with. She said, yeah, she was with my mother when I was born. I was out here in the country. I can't remember her name now. And so I was, I wish I had kept track of everybody I was with. Oh, it had been thousands I think. I really was with a lot of oldies.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Because I remember at the hospital in, you know, was it in Moscow? Yeah, I guess it was in Moscow. Well, maybe it was important. I don't know. Well, anyway, by 11 o 'clock I had delivered three babies. Three mothers came in. The doctors were there to help though. So I called her. They came and I could tell. I said, so I looked around and see if there was anybody around. I just addressed her right in the hall and brought her out into the delivery room. It wasn't time for anything else. So they brought her on the delivery room table. Otherwise they'd like to give them baths before they bring her in. But there was no time for that. I called the doctor and he was kind of mad. She said, I had a hunch I had to come in. I said, don't you know? No, I just have a hunch, but I better go. And she hardly got there.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: I know I delivered one baby. There was a nurse she had. It took two, three years of training, or two years, I guess, and quit. And I was just going on duty at seven o 'clock in the morning. And this nurse said there, and they yelled at me, you better come and see what's doing here. So I said, oh, is it you in there? Then why are you over here? I said, I'm ready to have a baby. I said, yes, but you can't go now. You'll have to deliver it right here. It was too late. So we delivered the baby, and they brought the stretcher in, so I could take her in. I asked the girl to bring a stretcher, and somebody's wrapped a blanket to wrap the baby in it. So they took that upstairs.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: You mean she was still outside?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: How many times you even put her on the stretcher… oh, my goodness.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah, it was funny experiences. Oh, yeah. Well, I know how fast it can happen, you know. So that was over with for them. It was funny, though. I said, ..., I said, didn't you know? Because she'd had two years of training. She said, no one was. She said they gave me some much medicine that I didn't know where I was. She didn't realize that she was going that fast. And I didn't know her while I was through and looked up her face. You had other things to worry about. I said, oh, my, did you win her? Oh, yes, she said, my. I said, well, we have to get the stretcher in. So I just had one of the girls get the stretcher and somebody to cut her blanket so you could take the baby in. And that was all. And she brought her upstairs, too. She had to be there for a while. Two days. She felt better.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But now they're bad. They don't let them stay in the hospital one day. No, they let me out. I think my baby was 32 hours old when I went home. Not much. Thirty-two hours. Oh, no. Just overnight. Marshall. Just overnight.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Yeah. I think that's a shame. My mother isn't ready to go home that quick. I know Dr. Laura told me, he said, it takes nine months to get that stomach sat big, and it doesn't go back in place in that big of a hurry, she said. It's no sense in it, he said. And he was mad about it. And he's dead enough, too. He had caught her right up in the paper body.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Well, when your mother had her babies, how long did she have to stay in bed?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Oh, I don't know. She had Dr. Gritman come out, funny. And then Dr. Asprey came and came on out. I really don't know. They sent us off to neighbors, so I really don't know much about it.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Yeah, they didn't want you to know, did they?

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell

speaker: Karen Purtee

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Well, I got married after a while, not too long afterwards. And then my husband died after ten months. And then I went back to nurses training in Portland, and I was there three years. And then I, they wanted me to take charge of the x-ray department. I did that for a year. But it was kind of hard. There was so much lifting. Patients with the limbs and backs. And I could hardly take it. And then they had to have treatment. They had to wheel them out to another place and up an incline. And I had to get help for that each time. Yeah, you're kind of small to be lifting people around. Yeah, and then give them the treatment and bring them back again. And some other, I saw it. It was kind of hard, so I quit that. So I'm back down here and had work at the Gritman.

speaker: Karen Purtee

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Well, they had an old building.This is a new building altogether now. Yeah. But they had an old building and they had some patients over there. After they built the first half. And she was ready to deliver. So we had to hurry down and help deliver her. And I remember he came back and said, Well, I was like a boy or a girl. He was interested now. He knew what we had to go for. So, but it went as funny as it went, as good as it did. I really, I, Marvelous, I think, it went so good for us.

words: Yeah. Because the old building, it had an incline to outside. Well, they had built over it, so it didn't braid on you. But it had an incline to the old building. And this new building is over here. And then we had all the old buildings and new patients over there. As many as we could handle over here. I see. So you had to spend your time rushing back and forth between the two buildings. Yeah, that's right. I took out one baby. There was a premature. We had to feed it by pushing a tube down in a throat for, I don't know how long. But I especially like those. Dr. Dunwater made it do it, so I did it. He said, Well, the government spends so much money foolishly. He said, You can use it as well. Spend it on what was on this.

words: So that's how I happened. I see one baby I took care of. Afterward, there was Dr. Wilson's patient. We had an incubator. We couldn't take it out. We had to do everything through a window. words: My goodness. That's rewarding, isn't it?

words: Yeah… it was kind of nice to see it. She lived up by the end of the sea.

She had an allergic to it and I said, oh, that's just all foolishness. So they gave her a dose and she couldn't have went out and gave me that respect to death. After that she said they never said that anymore.

words: There's a lot of people that are supposed to be allergic to it.

speaker: Hanna Anderson Sandell
words: Well, I had one man there that had penicillin four years before and they gave him penicillin and he was allergic to it then. But he wasn't the first four years ago. He was all right. So it shows that you can't always tell the year you're taking it. Your body changes all the time, they say. I sure is a lot of changes. A lot of them just try and see if it works. Well, of course, that's the way to learn, but they have tried on dogs or something like that first, I think. Yeah. And there's people that scream about that, too.
